name: Palace of Culture and Science
label: Palace of Culture
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plac Defilad' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plac Defilad' (way/257924765): middle (437 m across); moved 30 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1319250: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palace of Culture and Science' (394 m across).
notes: Warsaw's best-known skyscraper in the city centre.

text.description: The Palace of Culture and Science is the tall, stepped tower that dominates central Warsaw. It was built between 1952 and 1955 to designs by the Soviet architect Lev Rudnev, who drew on American art deco skyscrapers and added Polish details, such as parapets modelled on Renaissance houses. At about 237 metres, it is still the second tallest building in Poland. It photographs well because it is so big and so symmetrical. Seen straight on from the square in front of it, the tower rises in a clean central line, with modern high-rises on either side. The details are worth a closer look too: statues of Nicolaus Copernicus and Adam Mickiewicz stand by the main entrance, and four clock faces, each 6.3 metres across, sit near the top. Since 2010 the building has been lit by LED lights that can change colour at night, so an evening shot can look quite different from a daytime one. For a phone, the easy win is the symmetrical, straight-on view from Plac Defilad. If you want a wider setting, Most Świętokrzyski gives you the palace within the skyline across the Vistula, with the river in the foreground. Park Świętokrzyski gives mid-distance shots with trees and benches around the tower. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean, and check the square for temporary fencing or stage works before you settle on a spot.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of Warsaw, on and around Plac Defilad, with the main facade facing the square. It is surrounded by modern high-rises.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the centre of Warsaw and the large square called Plac Defilad, by taxi or hired scooter. The palace is hard to miss given its height. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) from where you stand, as the tower is very tall and you will be very close. Use the default lens (1x) if you step further back, and telephoto (2x-5x) for the clock faces, the statues or the spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plac Defilad (in front of the main facade, centred on the tower). The whole tower framed straight on, with modern high-rises on either side, ideal for a symmetrical shot. You will be very close, so use the ultra-wide lens and expect to tilt the phone upward. For the classic whole-tower, straight-on view with modern high-rises on either side, Plac Defilad in front of the main facade is the recommended general viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the tower's central spire up with the middle vertical line for a symmetrical shot. Standing close and shooting upward with the ultra-wide gives a dramatic, towering look, but keep the phone as upright as you can, as tilting it back makes the sides lean inwards. For a different view, try Most Świętokrzyski, which shows the palace within the skyline with the river in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the building does not wash out. At night, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your own body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour or sunset, when the building is lit against the sky.

text.access_note: Plac Defilad and the surrounding public spaces are open areas, but the palace's inside attractions, such as the 30th-floor terrace, theatres and museums, may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Warsaw Uprising Museum
label: Uprising Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Muzeum Powstania Warszawskiego' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/167109428: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Warsaw Rising Museum' (222 m across).
notes: Museum in a former tram power station with a brick tower.

text.description: The Warsaw Uprising Museum sits in the Wola district and tells the story of the 1944 uprising. The building is a converted brick industrial power station. The facade and entrance on Grzybowska 79 are the easiest place to take a clean picture, with the Wola streetscape and some nearby towers around it. The museum was set up as an institution in 1983 and opened on 31 July 2004, the 60th anniversary of the uprising. Inside there are exhibits over several floors, and a hall with a full-size B-24 Liberator. Outside, the museum's grounds (Freedom Park) have a memorial wall of names, a replica of the Kubuś armoured car and more than 30 colourised photo posters, which make good foregrounds or backgrounds if you have time to walk around. For a phone photo, start at the entrance and take one wide shot of the whole facade, then move closer for details such as the brickwork and the doorway. Keep the entrance clear so other visitors can get in and out. Photography rules inside can vary by exhibition, so follow the staff signs, and check the official site before you go for anything about tickets or access.
text.geographic_location: In the Wola district of Warsaw, on Grzybowska 79, in a former tram power station among modern towers and city streets.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to Grzybowska 79 in the Wola district. The phone icon on the map marks the middle of the museum's outline, not the entrance. The facade and street-facing entrance are on Grzybowska 79, so walk to them for your main shot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole brick facade and the entrance in one frame, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for brick texture and doorway details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the facade shot, walk to the street-facing entrance on Grzybowska 79. From there the photo shows the former tram power station's brick facade and entrance, set against the Wola streetscape and nearby towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the facade with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean. Keep the entrance in the lower part of the frame and let the sky and towers sit above. If you want a second view, Freedom Park, the museum's outdoor grounds, gives you the memorial wall of names, the replica armoured car and the colourised posters in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the brick keeps its texture. Hold the phone steady and keep the entrance clear of other visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the official site for current opening times.

text.access_note: The exterior and entrance area can be photographed from the street, but the museum itself is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go.

name: Royal Castle
label: Royal Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plac Zamkowy' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plac Zamkowy' (way/133637274): middle (259 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/64436: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Royal Castle' (184 m across).
notes: Reconstructed royal residence on Castle Square.

text.description:
The Royal Castle stands on Castle Square at the entrance to Warsaw's Old Town. It was a royal residence and seat of government, and today it is a state museum. It began in the 14th century as a home for the Dukes of Masovia. Under Sigismund III Vasa in the early 1600s it was enlarged into the Mannerist-Baroque building you see now. The castle was badly damaged in 1939 and deliberately blown up by German forces in September 1944. After a decision in 1971 it was rebuilt from surviving fragments, documents and rescued artworks, and the interiors reopened to the public in 1984.

It photographs well because of the bright red front and the open square in front of it. The classic picture is the red castle facade with Sigismund's Column in the foreground and Old Town rooftops behind. Stand on the square's edge near Krakowskie Przedmieście, or on the Old Town side. The square is free to enter, so you can take your time and try a few angles.

For a change, Świętojańska street gives a view of cobblestones leading to the red facade, with the square opening up beyond. The castle gardens are a quieter, greener alternative with plants in the frame. Whichever spot you pick, keep the phone level so the long building doesn't lean.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Warsaw, on Castle Square (Plac Zamkowy) at the entrance to the Old Town. The castle is part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Centre of Warsaw.
text.directions_text: Start from the Old Town and walk to Castle Square (Plac Zamkowy), where the castle's red front faces the open square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the castle, the column and the sky into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the facade or the rooftops behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plac Zamkowy (edge near Krakowskie Przedmieście, or the Old Town side of the square). The red castle facade framed with Sigismund's Column in the foreground, with the Old Town rooftops in the background. From here the red castle facade is framed by Sigismund's Column in the foreground, with the Old Town rooftops behind. The castle lies to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the column on one third of the frame, with the red facade filling the rest. Keep the phone upright and level so the building doesn't lean. For a different view, try Świętojańska street for the cobblestone lead-in to the facade, or the castle gardens for a greener, quieter picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour is the time for the illuminated castle. Dawn gives an emptier square.

text.access_note: The square is free to enter.
additional_notes: Interior photography is usually allowed only without flash, and some exhibitions do not allow photos; check on the day.
Tripods are discouraged or restricted in some places, and drone flying is typically restricted around the castle.
Holding a phone against a wall or railing helps keep it steady for night shots.
The gardens are quieter than the square, and their exact name on the map should be checked.

name: National Stadium
label: National Stadium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Most Poniatowskiego' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Most Poniatowskiego' (node/1285567449): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/435894154: large area 'National Stadium in Warsaw' (791 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Red-and-white stadium on the east bank of the Vistula.

text.description:
The National Stadium is Warsaw's big football and concert arena, and it is easy to recognise. Its outer skin is silver and red, meant to recall a waving Polish flag, and the same colours run through the seating inside. The stadium was built between 2008 and November 2011 on the site of the old 10th-Anniversary Stadium. It seats 58,580 for football, which makes it the largest football arena in Poland, and it hosted matches at UEFA Euro 2012. A tall central spire rises above the pitch, about 124 metres above the Vistula, and the roof hangs from it.

The stadium photographs best as a whole building rather than a close-up. The long, curved facade is one clean shape, and the red-and-white panels stand out against the sky. You see the full front with the bridge running alongside it, which is the classic view of the arena.

Keep your phone level so the long horizontal lines stay straight, and wait for a gap in the traffic if the bridge is busy. If you want a different angle, the notes below suggest two more places across the city. Check current access and any event-day closures around the stadium before you go.
text.geographic_location: The stadium is in the Praga Południe district on the east bank of the Vistula, close to the city centre, on Zieleniecka Avenue. The Poniatowski Bridge runs alongside it.
text.directions_text: Head for Most Poniatowskiego from the city centre by road, as no station or tram stop is listed for this spot. If you want to see the stadium up close, walk north-east towards it and keep it in view ahead of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the whole facade and the bridge fit in one frame. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the red-and-white panels and the spire. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is only worth trying if you walk much closer to the stadium.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Most Poniatowskiego (Approach from the bridge's side toward the stadium). The full front facade of the stadium with the Poniatowski Bridge alongside it, a typical composition for the arena. Approaching from the side of the bridge. From there you see the full front facade of the stadium with the bridge alongside it, which is the typical composition for the arena.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the stadium's long edge up with a horizontal line so the building does not lean. Let the bridge's edge lead the eye towards the stadium. For a different view, try Plac Zamkowy, which shows the red-and-white arena in the distance from the Royal Castle square, or Most Świętokrzyski, where the stadium's crown rises above the bridge with the Vistula in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stadium to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the red panels keep their colour. Take a few shots in a row, as vehicles on the bridge can spoil a frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before noon, when the light falls on the east-facing panels.

text.access_note: The bridge view is from a public road, but check the official site before you go for event-day closures and for details of any paid tour or upper-level viewing point at the stadium.

name: Presidential Palace
label: Presidential Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Krakowskie Przedmieście' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Krakowskie Przedmieście nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/855256739: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Presidential Palace' (193 m across).
notes: Official residence of the president on Krakowskie Przedmieście.

text.description: The Presidential Palace is the official residence of Poland's president, and its long, pale neoclassical front is a prominent landmark on Krakowskie Przedmieście. The building began in 1643 as a grand private mansion. The classical exterior you see today was shaped by the architect Chrystian Piotr Aigner from 1818, with a colonnade, balustrade and stone statues along the top. Four stone lions guard the courtyard on the street side. The palace has been home to the head of state since July 1994, and it came through the 1944 Warsaw Uprising intact. It photographs well because the whole width fits in one frame if you stand a little way back across the boulevard. The equestrian Poniatowski statue in the forecourt gives the picture a clear focal point. Keep the palace as the main subject and let the street and trees frame it. For a closer shot, zoom in on the statue with the façade behind it, or on the lions and the gate. You can only see the exterior. The grounds and gate are a security zone, so stay outside the perimeter and follow the guards' instructions. For a second angle, the terrace at St. Anne's church looks down the boulevard towards the palace. Check that it is open before you climb up.
text.geographic_location: The palace stands on Krakowskie Przedmieście in central Warsaw, a short distance from the Royal Castle and Sigismund's Column.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Krakowskie Przedmieście, the boulevard near the Royal Castle and Sigismund's Column. Look for Hotel Bristol, which is a handy landmark. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the boulevard. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the pavement is busy and you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statue, lions and gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Krakowskie Przedmieście (opposite the palace, across the boulevard near Hotel Bristol, a few steps back from the façade). The full neoclassical width of the palace front with its colonnade, framed by the boulevard, with the Poniatowski statue visible in the forecourt. Opposite the palace across the boulevard near Hotel Bristol, a few steps back from the façade. From here the full width of the colonnaded front fits in the frame, with the Poniatowski statue in the forecourt.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the palace's vertical columns and roofline, and keep the phone level so the building doesn't lean. Let the boulevard frame the shot. Then take a tighter second frame of the statue against the façade, with the lions and guards at the gate as small extra details. For a high-up view down the street, the terrace at St. Anne's church is an alternative; check access first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace front to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the pale stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as people and vehicles pass through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the street is quiet and the light falls across the front from the east. Late afternoon gives softer light.

text.access_note: You can only see the exterior of this working presidential residence from outside the security perimeter, so follow the guards' instructions. One guide reports a changing of the guard at noon on Saturdays and national holidays, so confirm locally before planning around it.

name: Wilanów Palace
label: Wilanów Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pałac w Wilanowie' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pałac w Wilanowie' (way/8106732): middle (143 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/8106732: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wilanow Palace' (144 m across).
notes: Baroque royal palace and gardens in the south of the city.

text.description: Wilanów Palace is a baroque royal residence in the south of Warsaw. It was built between 1677 and 1696 for King John III Sobieski, to a design by Augustyn Wincenty Locci. It is laid out in the French way, with a formal entrance courtyard at the front and the garden behind. From the courtyard you see the yellow-and-white main façade straight on, decorated with sculpted trophies and royal emblems that celebrate the king and his military victories. Guides call this the most photographed palace view in Poland, and it is easy to see why: the building is symmetrical, the colours are strong, and the courtyard gives you room to step back. The palace came through the Second World War and was reopened to the public in 1962. Its museum dates from 1805, and around 3 million people visited in 2019, so expect company. For a phone, the aim is to fit the whole façade in and then pick out a few details. Start with a wide shot from the courtyard, then zoom in on the reliefs and statues. If you have time, two other views are worth a look. The upper terrace looks over the formal garden with the palace behind, and the lake shows the palace across the water, framed by trees. Check the garden and park arrangements before you go, as some areas need a ticket.
text.geographic_location: Wilanów Palace is in the Wilanów district in the south of Warsaw. It stands with its park and formal gardens around it and the Wilanów lake nearby.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Wilanów district, south of the city centre, and reach it by taxi or hired scooter. Ask to be set down at the palace's main entrance gate. From the gate, walk straight into the front courtyard. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) to get the whole yellow-and-white façade in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the sculpted trophies and emblems.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front courtyard, approach from the entrance gate). The yellow-and-white baroque main façade seen straight on from the entrance courtyard, with its sculpted trophies and royal emblems. In the front courtyard on the approach from the entrance gate. From here the palace's main façade is in front of you, seen straight on, with its sculpted trophies and royal emblems.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the centre of the façade with the middle vertical line, so the symmetry looks deliberate. Keep your phone level so the walls do not lean. Then zoom in for a second shot of the carved details. If you would like a different view, the terrace over the formal garden and the lakeside view of the palace across the water are both alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale yellow and white do not wash out. If a lot of people are in the courtyard, take a few frames a few seconds apart and keep the cleanest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a bright day when the sun is not directly overhead, such as mid-morning or late afternoon. Arriving early usually means fewer people in the courtyard.

text.access_note: The courtyard approach is the usual way in, but parts of the park and gardens may need a ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Warsaw Barbican
label: Barbican
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Podwale' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Podwale nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/249395313: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Warsaw Barbican' (35 m across).
notes: Brick fortified gate at the edge of the Old Town.

text.description:
The Warsaw Barbican is a rounded brick outpost on the edge of the Old Town, standing between the Old and New Towns. It guarded the gate on Nowomiejska Street and was built in 1540 to a design by Jan Baptist the Venetian. It is about 14 metres wide and 15 metres high measured from the bottom of the moat, and it juts out around 30 metres from the walls. It was rarely used in a fight. The one recorded occasion was in 1656, during the Swedish invasion. Most of what you see is a rebuild from 1952 to 1954, made after wartime destruction using old etchings as a guide, with bricks salvaged from buildings in Nysa and Wrocław.

It photographs well because the shapes are simple and strong: a curved bastion, towers, a gateway and a stretch of the old moat in front. The warm brick stands out against the sky, and the moat gives you a foreground. The best-known view is from the street called Podwale, looking up at the bastion from below the walls, and guides recommend the morning light. If you want a calmer angle, Plac Krasińskich shows the Old Town walls and the Barbican across an open square, and Nowomiejska gives you the brick towers against the rooftops of Freta Street. Take a few frames from each and compare them later.
text.geographic_location: In Warsaw's Old Town, on its northern edge where it meets the New Town. It stands at the end of Nowomiejska Street, beside the surviving stretch of the old city walls.
text.directions_text: Head for the northern edge of the Old Town, where it meets the New Town, and look for the round brick bastion beside the walls. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the bastion, the gateway and the moat into one frame from the street. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the brick texture and the tops of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Podwale (moat side, facing the round bastion from the street below the walls). The rounded brick bastion and gateway rising beside the surviving stretch of the old moat, framed from street level. On the moat side, facing the round bastion from the street below the walls. From here you see the rounded brick bastion and gateway rising beside the old moat.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the moat in the lower third, with the bastion filling the middle and the sky above. Keep the phone level, otherwise the walls will lean. For a different view, try Plac Krasińskich for a more open, quieter angle across the square, or Nowomiejska for the towers against the Freta Street roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the brick to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. If the sun is behind the walls, tap the shaded brick and lower the exposure slightly. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when guides say the light is best for this view from Podwale.

text.access_note: The Barbican passage and the walls can be visited at any time, but the interior exhibition only runs in some seasons and the walkway on top depends on the weather, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Taking the photo with the phone held level helps keep the walls from appearing to lean.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the sky from washing out when the sun is behind the walls.
Night mode works best if the phone is braced against a wall or railing.

name: Palace on the Isle
label: Łazienki Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Agrykola' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Park Agrykola' (way/390489497): middle (421 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1325609735: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palace on the Isle' (109 m across).
notes: Neoclassical palace on a lake in Łazienki Park.

text.description: The Palace on the Isle, also called the Palace on the Water or Łazienki Palace, sits on an artificial island in a lake inside Royal Łazienki Park. That setting is what makes it easy to photograph. You get a pale neoclassical building with water in front of it and trees around it, and the park is open and easy to walk through. It began as a Baroque bathhouse, built between 1683 and 1689 for Prince Stanisław Herakliusz Lubomirski. King Stanisław August Poniatowski bought the estate in 1764 and had the building turned into his summer residence. The work went on in stages, and the palace had its present neoclassical look by the 1790s. German forces set it on fire in 1944. It was rebuilt and reopened to the public in 1960. From the Agrykola bridge you look across the water towards the palace's facade, so the island and the greenery fit in one frame. If the water is calm, a reflection may be possible too. A second, more distant view comes from the Amphitheatre side of the park, which shows the palace small among water and trees. Bring a lens cloth for your phone, as park paths can be dusty. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, then pick the one where the building sits level and the water fills the lower part of the picture.
text.geographic_location: The palace is inside Royal Łazienki Park in Warsaw, on an artificial island in the park's lake.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for Royal Łazienki Park in Warsaw and check the map for the route. Make for the Agrykola bridge on the park's water, then look south-east towards the island. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the palace, the water and the trees all fit in the frame. Then try the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to bring the facade closer without walking nearer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground water, and keep the palace near the middle of the frame, because the edges of an ultra-wide shot can stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Agrykola (bridge carrying Agrykola street over the park water, shooting toward the palace on the island). The palace on its island across the pond, framed from the bridge and looking toward the palace's facade. From here you look south-east across the water to the palace on its island, with the facade facing you. The palace sits some way off, so it will look fairly small at 1x. The exact spot on the bridge may differ from what you expect, so check the map before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the palace on one of the upper lines, with the water filling the lower third. Keep the horizon level, and keep the bridge rail out of the frame or use it as a foreground line. If the water is calm, include some of the reflection. For a different view, walk to the Amphitheatre side of the park, where the palace appears further off with the water and greenery around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale walls and the sky don't turn white. Take a few frames at 1x and at 2x-3x, and keep the best. Hold the phone against the rail or press your elbows to your sides to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is a good bet, when the park is quieter and the water is often calmer for a reflection. A bright, overcast day also works, because it keeps the light even on the pale facade.

text.access_note: Royal Łazienki Park and the palace exterior are free to enter, but interior visits are ticketed and photo rules inside vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Saxon Garden
label: Saxon Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plac Marszałka Józefa Piłsudskiego' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plac marszałka Józefa Piłsudskiego' (way/4969141): point nearest the subject (160 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4943389: large area 'Saxon Garden' (747 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Oldest public park in Warsaw, with a fountain and pavilion.

text.description:
The Saxon Garden (Ogród Saski) is a 15.5-hectare public park in central Warsaw, facing Piłsudski Square. It is the oldest public park in the city, and it opened to the public on 27 May 1727, which made it one of the first parks in the world that anyone could walk into. It began as a formal Baroque garden in the French style, and in the 19th century it was reshaped into a softer English-style landscape park. It was badly damaged during and after the Warsaw Uprising and has been partly rebuilt since. Around 20 of its old sandstone statues survive. The long central alley is decorated with sculptures.

For photos, the best starting point is the square at the garden's edge. The arches of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, with the eternal flame beneath them, make a strong foreground. The open square behind gives the shot room to breathe. Step back a little so the scale of the arches and the square both show. The guard changes every hour, which gives you a lively moment to photograph, but keep clear of the guards and be aware that mourners may be present.

Once you have your shot, walk into the garden. The central fountain and sculpture, set against trees and paths, make a calm second picture. The long shaded avenue of trees and statues is good for a receding view, and for seasonal colour.
text.geographic_location: In the Śródmieście district, central Warsaw. The garden lies just beside Piłsudski Square. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier arcade is on Piłsudski Square at the garden's edge.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so start from central Śródmieście and head to Piłsudski Square. From there the middle of the garden is to the south-west, about 4 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the arches and the square. If you can't step back far enough to fit the whole arcade, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the guard or for details of the statues in the garden.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plac Marszałka Józefa Piłsudskiego (in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier arcade, facing the arches). The Tomb's arches and eternal flame framed in the foreground, with the open square spreading out in front of them. In front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier arcade, facing the arches. From here the photo shows the arches and the eternal flame framed in the foreground, with the open square spreading out in front of them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Back off a little so the arches and the square both fit, and turn on gridlines to keep the columns straight. Tap the arches to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright. In the garden, a second option is the central fountain with greenery behind it. Another is the long tree-lined avenue of statues, with the path leading the eye into the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone level so the arches don't lean. If you want the guard change, hold still and take a Live Photo or a burst. Keep well back and out of the guards' way.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is calmer, with fewer people in frame. Late afternoon is softer on the stone.

text.access_note: The garden is a public park, open from dawn to dusk, but check the official site before you go. The Tomb is a place of remembrance, so keep clear of the guard.

name: Nowy Świat Street
label: Nowy Świat
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Krakowskie Przedmieście' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Krakowskie Przedmieście and Nowy Świat (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Elegant pedestrian-friendly street of cafés on the Royal Route.

text.description: Nowy Świat is one of Warsaw's main historic streets and part of the Royal Route, which links the Royal Castle and Old Town with the old royal residence at Wilanów. It photographs well because it is a long, fairly straight street lined with low neoclassical frontages, so the rooflines and shop fronts lead the eye into the distance. The classic picture is taken from the junction with Krakowskie Przedmieście. Here the Copernicus statue stands in the foreground and the street runs away behind it. The street looks old, but almost all of it was destroyed in the Warsaw Uprising of 1944. Afterwards it was rebuilt to look as it did in the early 19th century, when stone and brick buildings of about three storeys replaced the earlier wooden manors. Today it is lined with shops, restaurants and cafes, so you will usually find people, café tables and signs in the scene. Use them to add life to the frame, but wait a moment for a clearer gap if you want the facades on their own. Keep the phone level so the building edges stay upright, and put the statue on one side rather than in the exact centre. For a second angle, try Plac Trzech Krzyży at the far end, where the facades draw in towards Krakowskie Przedmieście, especially when the street lamps are lit in the early evening.
text.geographic_location: In central Warsaw, on the Royal Route. Nowy Świat runs from Three Crosses Square northwards and turns into Krakowskie Przedmieście near the Warsaw University campus and the Copernicus monument.
text.directions_text: From Castle Square by the Royal Castle, walk south along Krakowskie Przedmieście until you reach the Copernicus monument near the Warsaw University campus. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the junction view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole statue and the facades on both sides. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pull the street's buildings closer together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Krakowskie Przedmieście and Nowy Świat (south end, by the Copernicus monument in front of Staszic Palace). Nowy Świat running away from the Krakowskie Przedmieście junction, with the Copernicus statue and the neoclassical facades in the foreground. Stand on Krakowskie Przedmieście, at the south end by the Copernicus monument in front of Staszic Palace, and point the phone south. From there you see Nowy Świat running away from the junction, with the Copernicus statue and the neoclassical facades in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the statue to one side as a foreground anchor and let the street lead the eye into the distance. Keep the phone level and turn on gridlines so the building edges stay upright. If you have time, Plac Trzech Krzyży at the other end of the street gives a second view of the facades drawing together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facades to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. At 0.5x, keep the statue away from the edge of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or the golden hour before sunset tends to give softer light and fewer people. In the early evening, the street lamps add atmosphere to the view from Plac Trzech Krzyży.

text.access_note: This is an open public street and junction, but check for events or closures before you go, as the street can be pedestrian-only on some summer weekends.
claims_not_in_sources: Nowy Świat is an open public street that can be visited at any time without a ticket.
Early morning and golden hour usually give softer light and fewer people on the street.
The street lamps are lit in the early evening and add atmosphere to the view from Plac Trzech Krzyży.
The street may be closed to traffic or pedestrian-only on some summer weekends, which can change the crowds and framing.
Cafe tables, signs and people are usually present along the street.

name: Old Town Market Place
label: Old Town Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rynek Starego Miasta' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rynek Starego Miasta' (relation/6458642): middle (164 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/435910025: 'Warsaw Mermaid', the best-known feature inside 'Market Square' (163 m across).
notes: Colourful rebuilt market square at the heart of the Old Town.

text.description: Old Town Market Place is the centre and oldest part of Warsaw's Old Town. It dates from the late 13th century, when Warsaw was founded, and was the heart of the whole city until the end of the 18th century. The pastel townhouses you see today are a careful rebuild. The square was blown up after the 1944 Warsaw Uprising and the houses were reconstructed between 1948 and 1953 to look as they did in the 17th century. It is a roomy square, about 90 by 73 metres, and each side is named after an 18th-century parliamentarian. On the north side you will find the Warsaw Historical Museum, and on the east side the Adam Mickiewicz Museum. In the square stands the bronze Warsaw Mermaid by Konstanty Hegel, which has been the symbol of the city since 1855. It photographs well because the ring of colourful, evenly spaced facades gives you a ready-made frame, and the Mermaid gives the picture a clear foreground. For a wider alternative, the northwest corner of the square lets you take in the whole sweep of houses in one shot. For a second, quieter view, the Barbakan gives a higher look over the Old Town rooftops and the square. Early morning is the best time if you want the square almost empty. Late afternoon suits you better if you prefer warmer light on the facades.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Warsaw's Old Town (Stare Miasto). The square is the centre of the district, with the townhouses forming a ring around it.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground station or tram stop at this spot, so head to the Old Town square, Rynek Starego Miasta (the Old Town Market Place). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole ring of facades into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the Mermaid with the houses behind her, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details on the facades.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rynek Starego Miasta (northwest corner of the square). A wide-angle view of the full sweep of the pastel townhouse facades around the square. From here you can frame the statue with the pastel townhouses behind. For an alternative wide-angle view of the full sweep of houses, walk to the northwest corner of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the edges of the houses up with the vertical lines so the facades stand straight. Keep the phone level, as tilting it will make the buildings lean. For a close-up, go to the Mermaid and shoot with the default lens (1x) so the bronze statue is in the foreground and the coloured facades rise behind it. For a higher, quieter view of the rooftops and the square, try the Barbakan instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky or bright walls look washed out. Use portrait mode on the Mermaid statue if you want the background softened.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dawn to 8 a.m. for a nearly empty square, or late afternoon for warm light on the facades.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space that can be visited at any time; museums on its sides are separate, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.

name: Warsaw Uprising Monument
label: Uprising Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plac Krasińskich' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plac Krasińskich' (way/462611073): middle (284 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1327606552: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Warsaw Uprising Monument' (25 m across).
notes: Bronze insurgent monument at Krasiński Square.

text.description:
This bronze group remembers the Warsaw Uprising of 1944. It was unveiled on 1 August 1989, the 45th anniversary of the uprising's outbreak. It stands about 10 metres tall and has two parts. The larger, raised part shows insurgents running into combat, with an abstract collapsing building behind them. The smaller part shows fighters climbing down into a manhole, a reference to the sewer journey that took thousands of insurgents out of the Old Town in September 1944, starting from this square. It was designed by Jacek Budyn and sculpted by Wincenty Kućma.

It photographs well because the figures are full of movement and the scene looks like a film still. The Supreme Court building, built behind it in 1999, gives a clean, plain backdrop that makes the dark bronze stand out. From the square you can take in the whole group in one frame. For a different view, walk up close and shoot upwards, so the figures seem to surge over you. You can also go round to the quieter back, where bas-reliefs show wartime posters and orders. Take your time at the front first, then explore the sides. Work calmly and keep other visitors' space in mind, as this is a memorial.
text.geographic_location: The monument is on the southern side of Krasiński Square (Plac Krasińskich) in Warsaw, with the Supreme Court building directly behind it.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so check a local journey planner for the best way to reach Krasiński Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full frontal view of the whole group. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close and want a dramatic upward angle. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for faces and details in the bronze.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plac Krasińskich (in front of the monument, on the square facing the bronze group, with the Supreme Court building behind). The full frontal view of the bronze insurgent group, with the Supreme Court building forming the backdrop. From here you get the full frontal view of the insurgents, with the Supreme Court building as the backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the group slightly off-centre, keeping the court building as a calm background. For an alternative, move close and hold the phone low at 0.5x so the figures rise above you. You can also try the quieter back of the monument, with its bas-reliefs of wartime posters and orders.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bronze to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the dark metal keeps its detail against the bright sky and building. Keep the phone level to avoid leaning verticals.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or overcast light works best, as harsh midday sun washes out the sculptural detail.

text.access_note: The monument stands in an open public square with no ticket needed, but check the official site before you go in case of any works or restrictions.

name: Sigismund's Column
label: Sigismund's Column
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plac Zamkowy' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plac Zamkowy' (way/133637274): middle (259 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/238615551: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sigismund's Column' (11 m across).
notes: Landmark column on Castle Square.

text.description: Sigismund's Column stands on Castle Square (Plac Zamkowy), next to the Old Town in Warsaw. A bronze king on a tall granite pillar is easy to photograph, and the red-brick Royal Castle behind it gives a strong, clear backdrop. The column was first put up in 1644 for King Władysław IV Vasa, to honour his father, Sigismund III Vasa, who moved Poland's capital from Kraków to Warsaw in 1596. The bronze king is 2.75 m tall and wears armour and a crown. He holds a cross in one hand and a sabre in the other. The column is adorned by four eagles. It was once red marble (the original marble shaft was about 8.5 m tall) and is now granite. The Germans brought the column down on 1 September 1944, during the Warsaw Uprising. The statue was repaired and set on a new granite column in 1949, a short way from the original spot. The square is part of the Historic Centre of Warsaw, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. For the classic picture, stand a few steps back from the base, so the column rises in front of the castle facade with the Old Town roofline beyond. Keep the column slightly off-centre and let the square's open space show its scale. Midday in summer is busy, so go early or in the late afternoon if you want fewer people in the frame. If you have time, a second view looks down Krakowskie Przedmieście towards the square.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Warsaw, on Castle Square (Plac Zamkowy), next to the Old Town. The Royal Castle faces the column, and the view down Krakowskie Przedmieście opens onto the square.
text.directions_text: Head for Castle Square, next to Warsaw's Old Town, and look for Plac Zamkowy and the Royal Castle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the column against the castle without distortion. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the whole square and the tall column in one shot. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter picture of the statue and the eagles.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plac Zamkowy (a few steps back from the base, facing the Royal Castle facade). The column rising in the foreground with the red-brick Royal Castle facade behind it and the Old Town roofline beyond. From there, walk south to Plac Zamkowy, then stand a few steps back from the base, facing the Royal Castle facade. From this spot the column rises in the foreground with the red-brick castle behind it and the Old Town roofline beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the column on one of the vertical lines, with the castle filling the background. Leave a little space around it so the scale of the square shows. For an alternative, move to Krakowskie Przedmieście and shoot down the street, using the facades on each side as a frame as the view opens onto the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the column to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly. This keeps the bright sky from washing out the bronze statue. Hold the phone upright so the column does not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 9 a.m. for fewer tour groups, or late afternoon for warm light on the castle facade. Midday in summer is the busiest time.

text.access_note: The column stands on an open public square; check the official site or local notices before you go in case of events or works.

name: Holy Cross Church
label: Holy Cross Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Świętokrzyska' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Świętokrzyska nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28092628: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Holy Cross Church' (87 m across).
notes: Baroque church holding Chopin's heart.

text.description: The Church of the Holy Cross is one of the most notable Baroque churches in Warsaw, with a twin-towered facade on the busy Krakowskie Przedmieście. It photographs well because the facade stays calm and symmetrical while the city moves around it, and in the evening, when it is lit, it stands out against a deep blue sky. The main building went up between 1679 and 1696 to a design by Józef Szymon Bellotti. The towers got their late Baroque tops in the early 18th century. Inside, a pillar holds the urn with the heart of Frédéric Chopin. The church was badly damaged in 1944 and blown up in January 1945. It was rebuilt between 1945 and 1953 in a simpler form, so what you see is a careful postwar rebuilding. Stand on the far pavement, look north and let the lit facade fill the middle of the frame, with the street lights and passers-by around it. If you want a daytime alternative, Krakowskie Przedmieście gives a straight-on view of the facade, and the Copernicus monument can sit in the foreground. Keep to the pavement, as the boulevard is busy with traffic.
text.geographic_location: In central Warsaw, on Krakowskie Przedmieście, opposite the main University of Warsaw campus.
text.directions_text: Head for Krakowskie Przedmieście in central Warsaw. The church stands opposite the main University of Warsaw campus. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole facade and some of the street. Move to 2x or the telephoto lens if you want the two towers to fill the frame. The ultra-wide (0.5x) only helps if you walk right up to the church, and it will lean the towers inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Świętokrzyska (from the opposite side of the street, the evening angle). The lit-up church against a deep blue evening sky, with the busy street around it. Stand on the far pavement from the church and look north. The photo shows the lit-up church against a deep blue evening sky, with the busy street around it. Pick your exact spot by eye along the pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the towers upright, with the church centred. Let the street and its lights fill the lower part of the frame to show how busy the place is. If you walk to Krakowskie Przedmieście, you can try the Baroque twin-towered facade with the Copernicus monument in front. Check the current view on the map first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the lit facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky stays deep blue and the lights do not burn out. As the light fades, try night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a lamp post to keep the picture sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the sky is a saturated blue and the church is lit up.

text.access_note: The church is an active Roman Catholic place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and photography rules inside; interior photography is generally allowed without flash, but not during services.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the church centred and the towers upright with gridlines helps avoid leaning verticals.
Night mode usually needs a steady hold, which bracing against the body or a lamp post can help with.
The ultra-wide lens tends to make tall buildings lean inwards when you stand close.
Świętokrzyska is south of the church, so looking north from the stand-here point faces the facade.

name: Monument to the Ghetto Heroes
label: Ghetto Heroes
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'plac Bohaterów Getta Warszawskiego' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/231919035: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pomnik Bohaterów Getta' (44 m across).
notes: Memorial to the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.

text.description:
The Monument to the Ghetto Heroes commemorates the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943. It stands where the first armed clash of the uprising took place, in what was once part of the ghetto. It was unveiled on 19 April 1948 and is about 11 metres tall. Nathan Rapoport sculpted it, working under the supervision of Leon Suzin. Part of the stone is labradorite, which came from German supplies ordered by Albert Speer in 1942 for planned Nazi monuments.

It photographs well because the two faces are so different. The west side has a bronze group of insurgents, men, women and children, with the leader Mordechai Anielewicz standing at the centre. The east side is a quieter stone relief of persecution, called 'Pochód na zagładę' (March to Annihilation). The tall stone wall behind the figures gives clean, simple backgrounds, and the open square lets you step back and fit a lot in. The POLIN museum stands opposite, and it makes a good backdrop when you frame wider.

Start with the bronze side, then walk round to the stone relief as a contrast. This is a memorial, so keep a respectful distance from other visitors and avoid close-up posing. It is especially important around commemorations such as the 19 April anniversary.
text.geographic_location: In the area that was once part of the Warsaw Ghetto. The monument stands in a square bordered by Anielewicza, Karmelicka, Lewartowskiego and Zamenhofa streets, directly opposite the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground or tram stop at this spot, so head for the former ghetto area and ask for the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews or for plac Bohaterów Getta Warszawskiego. The monument stands in the square directly opposite the museum, so you can't miss it once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bronze relief and the monument as a whole. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and need to fit the full height and the plaza. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the faces and figures in the relief.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on plac Bohaterów Getta Warszawskiego. From here the plaza and the POLIN museum opposite frame the monument. For a second view, walk round to the quieter stone relief 'Pochód na zagładę' on the other side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the bronze group slightly off-centre, with the stone wall rising behind it. Keep the phone level so the vertical edges stay straight. Then take a tighter 2x or 3x shot of the central figure. As an alternative, shoot the stone relief on the other side, which is calmer and more sombre. Wait for a gap between visitors rather than asking anyone to move.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bronze figures to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the bronze keeps its detail and the stone doesn't wash out. Portrait mode is not needed here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early or late daylight, when stronger shadows bring out the detail in the relief.

text.access_note: The monument stands in an open public square and needs no ticket; if there is a commemoration event, check the official site before you go.

name: Chopin Monument
label: Chopin Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pomnik Fryderyka Chopina' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Fryderyka Chopina' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OSM W1448330230 (Frédéric Chopin Monument): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Art Nouveau statue of Chopin under a willow in Łazienki Park.

text.description:
The Chopin Monument is a seated bronze figure of the composer, set beneath a stylised willow in Łazienki Park. In front of it lies a still pond, and that pond is the reason the spot works so well for phones. The water mirrors the figure and the trees behind, so one simple shot gives you the statue, the willow and a soft reflection together. Guides often call it one of Warsaw's most photographed sights, and the view across the pond is the usual way to frame it.

Stand at the front, facing the sculpture across the water, and begin with the full view: the composer, the willow branches above him and the reflection below. Once you have that, move in for a tighter picture of the bronze surface, its textures and the inscriptions on the plinth. If you look up from a low angle, the willow branches make a natural frame around the figure.

The benches and lawn in front fill up on Sunday summer concert days, so people will probably appear in your frames unless you come early or late. One visitor reported conservation works that limited the view, so look for scaffolding before you plan your shot. A second option is the monument seen through the park gate from Aleje Ujazdowskie, which shows the statue with the greenery of its park setting around it.
text.geographic_location: The monument stands inside Łazienki Park in Warsaw. It can also be seen through the park gate from Aleje Ujazdowskie.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Walk through Łazienki Park to reach the monument and its pond. Once you can see the water and the willow, you are at the right place for the front view, standing at the front and facing the sculpture across the water. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full statue, willow and reflection. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the bronze details and inscriptions. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the benches or crowds force you to stand very close.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front, facing the sculpture across the pond). The seated bronze composer under the stylised willow, with the still water in front reflecting the figure and the trees behind. Facing the sculpture across the pond. From here you see the seated bronze composer under the stylised willow, with the still water in front reflecting the figure and the trees behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one third of the frame, with the pond filling the lower part so the reflection is included. Wait for the water to settle between breezes. For a second shot, zoom in on the bronze and the plinth inscriptions, using the willow branches as a frame from below. As an alternative, shoot from Aleje Ujazdowskie through the park gate to show the monument among the greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bronze figure to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and water do not wash out the detail. Keep the phone level so the horizon of the pond stays straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is suggested, as there are fewer people and the light is calmer. Before or after the Sunday summer concerts is also quieter.

text.access_note: The monument is in Łazienki Park and is free to view, but conservation works have been reported, so check for scaffolding before you go.

name: Multimedia Fountain Park
label: Fountain Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Skwer I Dywizji Pancernej' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Skwer 1 Dywizji Pancernej WP' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OSM W238861833 (Multimedia Fountain Park): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Evening water, light and music shows near the Old Town.

text.description: The Multimedia Fountain Park is a set of fountains with a projection screen behind them, set below the escarpment, with the Old Town rooftops and church towers visible behind it. It is a good place for phone photos because you can look down on the whole display from the rise at the edge of Skwer I Dywizji Pancernej, with Old Town rooftops and church towers behind the water. Guides call this the best postcard view of the park. The shows run only on Friday and Saturday evenings from May to September, and the park itself is free. In winter there have been illuminations, but they were listed for 2025/2026 only, so check whether they return. For the classic picture, stand on the raised ground at the square's edge and keep the fountains in the lower half of the frame and the skyline above. The last light before sunset is the loveliest moment, because the Old Town rooftops catch the light. If you want a street-level view instead, try ulica Rybaki. From there the fountains and the screen sit against the church silhouettes on the escarpment. Arrive early on show evenings, as the best spots fill up. Photographers can be barred from shooting during performances if this is announced, so be ready to put your phone away.
text.geographic_location: In Warsaw, in a park below the escarpment, with the Old Town rooftops and church towers visible behind the fountains from the square's raised edge.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground stop is listed for this spot, so start from Warsaw's Old Town, the skyline you will see behind the fountains, and go to the park below the escarpment. Once there, head for the raised ground on the edge of Skwer I Dywizji Pancernej, above the fountains. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole display and the skyline in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view, and to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the church towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Skwer I Dywizji Pancernej (elevated ground on the square's edge, above the fountains). The full fountain display from above, with Old Town rooftops and church towers behind it. On Skwer I Dywizji Pancernej, on the elevated ground at the square's edge, above the fountains. From there you see the full fountain display from above, with the Old Town rooftops and church towers behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the fountains on the lower third, with the rooftops and towers along the upper third. For a different version, walk to ulica Rybaki, where the fountains and the projection screen sit in front of the church silhouettes on the escarpment. Check the exact standing spot when you arrive, because that viewpoint is the escarpment above the park, not a separate square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountains to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright water and lights do not wash out. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the water, and rest your elbows on a rail or wall to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The last light before sunset, when the Old Town rooftops are lit. On Friday and Saturday evenings from May to September, arrive early for a good spot, since the shows draw a crowd.

text.access_note: This is an open, free park, but shows run only on Friday and Saturday evenings from May to September and photography can be restricted during performances, so check the official site before you go.

name: St. Anne's Church
label: St. Anne's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Krakowskie Przedmieście' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Krakowskie Przedmieście nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25865144: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Anne's Church' (84 m across).
notes: Church on the Royal Route with a bell tower popular for views.

text.description:
St. Anne's Church stands on Krakowskie Przedmieście, right beside Castle Square, and its pale Neoclassical front is one of the tidiest church facades in the Old Town area. The face you see today dates from 1788 and was designed by Chrystian Piotr Aigner. Statues of the Four Evangelists, carved by Jakub Monaldi and Franciszek Pinck, decorate it. The church itself is much older. It was founded in 1454 by Duchess Anna Fiodorowna for Bernardine friars, and it has been rebuilt several times since. That mix of old foundations and a calm, symmetrical front is what makes it rewarding to photograph.

The simplest picture is the front facade seen straight on from the street, with the doorway in the centre and the statues above it. Because the front is so symmetrical, a straight-on view looks neat and balanced. If you want something wider, the separate bell tower and the Mariensztat side give different views of the church. The tower terrace looks over Castle Square, Sigismund's Column and the Royal Castle.

The church is closed to visitors during Mass, so plan your visit around that. Early morning is a good time for the street, with fewer people around Castle Square and cleaner exterior shots.
text.geographic_location: St. Anne's Church is in Warsaw's historic centre, at Krakowskie Przedmieście 68, next to Castle Square. It sits on Krakowskie Przedmieście, next to Castle Square.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground or tram stop right at this spot, so head for Castle Square in the Old Town. The church is next to the square at Krakowskie Przedmieście 68. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade straight on. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is too narrow to fit the whole front in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Evangelist statues and the details above the door.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Krakowskie Przedmieście (on the street directly in front of the church's main facade). The baroque front facade of the church seen straight on from the boulevard.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the central doorway up with the middle vertical line so the symmetry shows. Keep the phone level to avoid the walls leaning inwards. Leave a little sky above the roofline. For a different view, the bell tower terrace looks over Castle Square with Sigismund's Column and the Royal Castle, and Mariensztat shows the church and tower from the other side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the pale stonework looks washed out against the sky. Take a few shots in a row so you can pick one without people walking through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the street is quieter and there are fewer people around Castle Square.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship and is closed during Mass, and the bell tower is a separate building, so check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements.

name: Nicolaus Copernicus Monument
label: Copernicus Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pomnik Mikołaja Kopernika' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Mikołaja Kopernika' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/282661680: the OpenStreetMap point 'Nicolaus Copernicus Monument'.
notes: Seated statue of the astronomer in front of the Staszic Palace.

text.description: Copernicus stands in bronze in front of the Staszic Palace on Krakowskie Przedmieście, holding a compass and an armillary sphere, the old model of the heavens. That is why the spot photographs well: a single dark figure against the long, pale classical facade of the palace is the standard Warsaw view of this monument. The statue was designed by Bertel Thorvaldsen in 1822 and finished in 1830, paid for by public donations and by Stanisław Staszic himself. It had a difficult 20th century. The Germans removed it after the 1944 Warsaw Uprising, but they were forced to retreat before they could melt it down. It came back to Warsaw in July 1945 and was unveiled again in 1949. In 2007 a bronze model of Copernicus's Solar System was added on the square in front, which gives you a nice foreground detail. The statue is often busy with visitors, so a little patience may be needed for a clear frame. Early morning or late afternoon is calmer. Take one wide shot to show the palace behind the figure, then move closer for a tighter picture of the statue and its instruments. The pedestal carries inscriptions in Latin on the east face and Polish on the west face, which are worth a close-up.
text.geographic_location: The monument stands on Krakowskie Przedmieście in central Warsaw, directly in front of the Staszic Palace, which is the seat of the Polish Academy of Sciences.
text.directions_text: Head for Krakowskie Przedmieście in central Warsaw and look for the Staszic Palace. The statue stands on the square in front of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue and the palace facade together. Switch to telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the figure and its compass, and use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole square, with the statue small in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front of the pedestal, facing the Staszic Palace across Krakowskie Przedmieście). The bronze figure framed against the classical Staszic Palace facade, the standard Warsaw composition for this monument. Walk west to the front of the pedestal and face the Staszic Palace across Krakowskie Przedmieście for the classic framing. From there the bronze figure sits against the palace facade. For a different view, try Krakowskie Przedmieście itself, looking down the street at the monument for a less crowded street scene, or the steps of Kościół Świętego Krzyża across the road, which show the palace and the monument together.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the palace's vertical edges with them so the building does not lean. Put the statue slightly off-centre and let the facade fill the background. If people stand around the base, wait a moment or crop in with the telephoto lens. Use the 2007 bronze Solar System on the square as a foreground detail if you want a wider shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the pale facade looks too bright or the bronze looks too dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when there are fewer people around the statue.

text.access_note: The monument stands in an open public space that is free to reach on foot at any hour.
claims_not_in_sources: Krakowskie Przedmieście and the Staszic Palace are in central Warsaw.
The statue is dark bronze against a pale facade, so the exposure slider may help.
The statue is often busy with visitors, so a clear frame may need some patience.

name: POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews
label: POLIN Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mordechaja Anielewicza' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Mordechaja Anielewicza and Ludwika Zamenhofa (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/186141946: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Polin Museum of the History of Polish Jews' (129 m across).
notes: Modern glass museum on the former Jewish ghetto site.

text.description:
POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews stands in Muranów, the prewar Jewish quarter of Warsaw, on the site of the former Warsaw Ghetto. It faces the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes. The Finnish architects Rainer Mahlamäki and Ilmari Lahdelma designed it, and it opened on 19 April 2013. The core exhibition followed on 28 October 2014. The plain, sand-coloured building is clad in glass fins and copper mesh, with the word Polin silk-screened on the glass in Latin and Hebrew letters. Inside, a tall entrance hall with an undulating wall is the main architectural feature.

It photographs well because the shapes are simple and strong. The curved stone wall, the large tree-shaped glass panel and the entrance all sit together in one angled view. The museum's own building guide points visitors to this junction to see the facade, so it is a sound choice for the architecture. The building sits in a park, so you can step back and look for cleaner lines. If you want the whole block with its glass fins and the cut-through entrance, walk to the Anielewicza and Karmelicka side. The museum faces a memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, so please take photos with respect.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Muranów, on the site of the former Warsaw Ghetto. It stands directly opposite the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so start from Muranów, the district around the museum. A bus stop is reported to be next to the site, but check a live journey planner for routes. Walk to the corner of Mordechaja Anielewicza by the main entrance. From there the museum building lies to the west, and the walk across to its middle is about 150 m, or roughly 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the curved stone wall, the tree-shaped glass panel and the entrance together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the facade in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for close shots of the glass fins and the lettering.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Mordechaja Anielewicza and Ludwika Zamenhofa (corner where the museum's triangular window and main entrance face the street junction). The curved stone wall, the large glass panel shaped like a tree, and the museum entrance, framed at an angle from the street corner. Stand on Mordechaja Anielewicza, at the corner where the museum's triangular window and main entrance face the street junction. From here you see the curved stone wall, the large glass panel shaped like a tree and the entrance, framed at an angle. Face west and the museum is in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building's vertical edges against the vertical lines so the walls do not lean. Let the curve of the wall lead the eye towards the entrance. For a wider view of the whole building with its glass fins and the cut-through entrance, try the alternative spot on the Anielewicza and Karmelicka side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky and the reflections in the glass do not wash out. Take a few shots at different zoom levels, as the glass reflects differently from each angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight suits the glass and stone best, and an overcast day cuts the glare. Early in the day there are usually fewer people on the pavement.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the public street and park. Photography inside the museum has its own rules (no flash or tripods, according to guides), so check the official site before you go.
